body: I have observed that this also happens with built-in callables. For example, if you subclass a `MultiMeshInstance2D` in an extension, which connects to the mesh instance's `changed` event, reloading the extension will randomly segfault when clearing instance state, specifically that signal connection.
I don't understand why this is classified as `documentation`, it should have `bug` and `crash` label.

I'm trying to think what we could do automatically within GDExtension to fix this?

We could keep track of all custom callables and destroy them when the GDExtension that created them is unloaded? But that would still "break" hot-reload if the extension was expecting those callables to still be valid after reload. But maybe that's the best we can do?

> I'm trying to think what we could do automatically within GDExtension to fix this?
> 
> We could keep track of all custom callables and destroy them when the GDExtension that created them is unloaded? But that would still "break" hot-reload if the extension was expecting those callables to still be valid after reload. But maybe that's the best we can do?

This is how i did it (keep track of the callables i've created, and on uninit, remove them). I dont think you would be able to keep them working, you have to break it (imagine a callable attached by a click of a button, it might have some context information, which might define which fn pointer to use).

I think its fair that the extension should re attach it callbacks when the `extension_reload` notification is given (also how i did it)

As far as I can tell, the problem is this:
- During construction, a custom callable specifies a set of callbacks like `free_func`, `call_func`, `equal_func`, `is_valid_func`, etc.
    - I'll call this "vtable" here.
    - In Rust, that looks [like this](https://github.com/godot-rust/gdext/blob/17f30e7e2544bcc821a2a4b2c8ca60d0dbe0bc8c/godot-core/src/builtin/callable.rs#L221-L231).
- Every custom callable has its own set of callbacks. I'm not sure why this is the case, but it has multiple disadvantages:
    - Every single custom `Callable` becomes invalid after reload (problem here).
    - Every single custom `Callable` needs to reserve its own memory for all the callbacks. For ~11 fields in `GDExtensionCallableCustomInfo`, this is at least 88 bytes. This can add up if games have lots of dynamic interactions, such as signals.
- After reload, the functions referenced by this callback may be on different addresses. This means any call through a previous `Callable` is instant UB.

Now, as a way forward, I see following options:
1. Mark all custom callables as invalid after reload. 
   - Possible, but means every user has to deal with this, which is non-trivial.
   - It would also be a discouraging factor to use custom callables vs. regular object-method ones.
1. After reload, iterate through all existing custom callables and call a "reinitialize" function that updates their callbacks.
   - Expensive, and would require central registry of all callables.
1. Let each callable store a _generation_, which is incremented by 1 on reload.
   - Invalid callables can be detected lazily, and their "reinitialize" can be triggered on demand.
1. Change the design, so that not every callable stores individual callbacks. Instead, the binding provides central callbacks once, which take the callable (or its `void*` user data) as a parameter.
   - This seems significantly more flexible. In fact I don't see what a per-callable vtable gives us -- it would still be possible to provide this with 1 level of indirection, using the new system: the central callback dispatches based on the callable's user data to the callable-specific callbacks. But this likely won't even be necessary.
   - It's still responsibility of the binding to keep the `void*` user-data valid, but that is possibly easier than the callbacks -- or we could find a way to serialize/retain it.
   - Would reduce bloat per callable. Even taking into account compatibility, we can box the vtable (`std::unique_ptr` etc). For callables using the new central system, this boxed pointer could just be null.

Thanks, @Bromeon! Your analysis makes sense

However, I still really can't visualize how a binding would be able to "reinitialize" a callable after reload. In godot-cpp, with custom callables created via `callable_mp()` or `callable_mp_static()` (which is the primary use of custom callables in godot-cpp), the core piece of data is a function pointer, which would be invalid as soon as the extension was unloaded. I don't know what metadata we could possibly store that would allow getting the equivalent function pointer once the extension was loaded again. If the function was bound, sure, we could look it up that way, but then the developer would use `Callable(obj, "method")` which isn't a custom callable

So, while we could adjust the API to make it easier to clean up custom callables when an extension is unloaded (or reduce the memory used, as you explained above), I just can't envision how we could do more than that. (Although, I think we also could pretty easily have Godot dispose of custom callables on extension unload without changing the API)

Or, is the situation somehow easier with the Rust bindings?

> However, I still really can't visualize how a binding would be able to "reinitialize" a callable after reload. In godot-cpp, with custom callables created via `callable_mp()` or `callable_mp_static()` (which is the primary use of custom callables in godot-cpp), the core piece of data is a function pointer, which would be invalid as soon as the extension was unloaded.

You're right, for us it's similar -- custom callables either point to functions (which may be at a different address after reload), or closures/lambdas (which also contain state that is now gone). So maybe invalidating the `Callable` is really the only way 🤔 

---

Not that this would solve the issue, but out of curiosity, do you know why we have a per-instance "vtable" (list of callbacks) in the first place? Was there a specific use case that mandated to store all function pointers _inside_ the `Callable`, rather than somewhere global, with a callable "ID" or "user data" being the distinguishing part?

> Not that this would solve the issue, but out of curiosity, do you know why we have a per-instance "vtable" (list of callbacks) in the first place? Was there a specific use case that mandated to store all function pointers inside the Callable, rather than somewhere global, with a callable "ID" or "user data" being the distinguishing part?


I guess you could argue why the vtable has so many ptrs, but you do need a vtable.
the only things i think could be smaller are:
* merging `equal_func` and `less_than_func` to `cmp_func` which returns -1/0/1
* merging `object_id` and `is_valid_func` as in my mind are there for the same reason, checking if the callable's context is still alive (the use could store the object in the `callable_userdata`, it would require making `is_valid_func` required though

In rust a callable would be represented with `Box<dyn Fn() + Display + PartialOrd + Hash + PartialEq + Drop>` plus more things (like `is_valid` and the `object_id`). Which would create pretty much the same vtable, just hidden from you.
If i may, also, having a global id would be a pain, callables can be created anywhere, so that global place would have to have a huge `match` or something to dispatch the correct `fn`, and each extension would have to come up with a system of dispatch, every new callable you want to create anywhere, would mean you have to go to that global place and add a new match branch.

Perhaps a mid-way solution would be the ability to register callable types (like we do with nodes), which would hold the vtable.
Then the user would be able to create `dynamic` callables (the current custom ones), or one of their own (which share the vtable)

Another way would be changing the create struct (`GDExtensionCallableCustomInfo2`) so that all funcs are passed as a pointer to a struct. That way extensions may box the vtable for one shots, and have a statically defined ones for the most common cases.
The vtable would need to be available, at least in the `free_func` so it can be dropped

> Not that this would solve the issue, but out of curiosity, do you know why we have a per-instance "vtable" (list of callbacks) in the first place? Was there a specific use case that mandated to store all function pointers _inside_ the `Callable`, rather than somewhere global, with a callable "ID" or "user data" being the distinguishing part?

I don't think there was a particular use-case in mind, I just don't think we considered this other possible design at the time. We were looking at the problem as allowing us to sub-class [`CallableCustom`](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/efb40c1524e54f2cf52f213e248bd0a7b790975a/core/variant/callable.h#L142) from Godot and implement each of its virtual methods. Providing a callback function for each of the virtual methods is the most direct way to do that :-) I think we also tend not to optimize for memory usage, except in specific cases where we think memory will be a big problem

That said, I don't know if anyone has found a use for the current design in the meantime, that wouldn't work with this alternative approach
Just found out that all signals in my project connected to custom callables have been deleted because of this bug. So I really want to bump this issue.
